items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: To name a few, there was ... Jonah Jones, the ex-Stuff Smith and Cab Calloway trumpet man

ctx.x: There was a bar called "Fat Mans" just under where Ulysses lived. Fat Mans' was Charles Turner and he played bass in Marion Hardy's Alabamians, the band that Cab Calloway came to New York with, and whom I played opposite at the Savoy with Scott. Fat Man and Eddie Mallory, a trumpet player with Hardy's band, had opened the bar together, but Fat Man eventually bought out Eddie's interest and was the sole owner. It was a very modern bar and became quite a hangout for musicians that mostly lived in the neighbourhood.

To name a few, there was Billy Taylor, the bass player, his son Billy, Jr., who also played bass, John Brown, a bass player, Jonah Jones, the ex-Stuff Smith and Cab Calloway trumpet man, Doles Dicksens, bass, Slick Jones, drummer on many Fats Waller recordings, Al Hall, bass, Gus Askins, trumpet, Leonard "Henn" Davis, trumpet, Bobby Sands, ex-Claude
Hopkins tenor man and the great Coleman Hawkins as well as Benny Carter.

items.title: 68728_Jonah
items.q: Bill Coleman said, "What's this? I ain't going to this." He said, "Go to that. Be sure you don't miss that." So he was getting me straight.

ctx.x: Getting invitations to the Painters' Exposition and stuff. Bill Coleman said, "What's this? I ain't going to this." He said, "Go to that. Be sure you don't miss that." So he was getting me straight. But I got back and things was really bad then. It was the end of '54. And I'm thinking about getting a job, because are getting up in size, so I said I have to have something coming in regular. So I had nothing but this little thing where we were going to Rochester and play. So we'd do that on the weekend. That was…
there. So that wasn't nothing. You do that one week, then you had to wait another month or two before you'd go again.
